chunks: And from him, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The boundary of the Rawdah (Garden) is from the Mosque of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) to the edge of the Zillal, and the boundary of the Mosque is to the two pillars on the right of the pulpit to the road from the side facing the Night Market.

key_terms.الرَّوْضَةِ: The Rawdah (Garden), a specific sacred area within the Prophet's Mosque in Medina.
key_terms.الطَّرِيقِ: The road, used here as a landmark for the boundary.
key_terms.الظِّلاَلِ: Al-Zillal, a specific location or structure in Medina marking the boundary of the Rawdah.
key_terms.سُوقَ اللَّيْلِ: The Night Market, a historical market in Medina used as a geographical reference.
key_terms.مَسْجِدِ النَّبِيِّ: The Mosque of the Prophet (Masjid al-Nabawi).

ai.seo_question: What are the defined boundaries of the Rawdah and the Prophet's Mosque according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* provides the precise topographical delimitation of the Rawdah al-Sharif, establishing it as the sacred space between the Prophet's pulpit and the Zillal (shaded areas), which holds significant jurisprudential weight for determining the status of prayer and visitation (*Ziyarah*) within these boundaries. By anchoring the boundaries to specific landmarks like the two pillars and the Night Market, it reflects the early scholarly efforts to preserve the physical sanctity of the Prophet's resting place as a locus of spiritual connection.
